Precise models predicting fuel cell performance under different operating conditions require accurate 
parameter identification in a proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC). Most traditional parameter 
estimation methodologies depend on optimization algorithms which are limited in their efficiency, 
convergence speed, and robustness. Typically, existing algorithms fail to achieve a balance between 
precision and computational efficiency, leading to suboptimal modeling of the complex, nonlinear 
behavior of PEMFCs. In this paper, we present the two-stage differential evolution (TDE) algorithm, 
which fills these gaps by using a new mutation strategy that improves solution diversity and speeds up 
convergence. Seven critical unknown parameters (ξ1, ξ2, ξ3, ξ4, β, RC, and λ) in PEMFC models are 
identified by using the proposed TDE algorithm. The optimization process is to minimize the sum of 
squared errors (SSE) between the experimentally measured and predicted cell voltages. TDE resulted 
in a 41% reduction in SSE (minimum SSE of 0.0255 compared to 0.0432), a 92% improvement in 
maximum SSE, and over 99.97% reduction in standard deviation compared to the HARD-DE algorithm. 
Furthermore, TDE was shown to be 98% more efficient than HARD-DE, with a runtime of 0.23 s, 
compared to HARD-DE’s runtime of 11.95 s. Extensive testing of these advancements was performed 
on six commercially available PEMFC stacks over twelve case studies, and I/V and P/V characteristics 
were confirmed to be consistent with experimental data. The results show that TDE has better 
accuracy, robustness and computational efficiency than the other methods, and therefore TDE can be 
used as a real time PEMFC parameter estimation tool.

Two main methods of modelling fuel cells are outlined in academic research. The first is the mechanistic model 
that attempts to closely mimic the heat and mass transfer, as well as the electrochemical reactions occurring in 
the fuel cells. The alternative approach is to use empirical or semi empirical models that estimate the effects of 
different input variables on the voltage current (V–I) characteristics of a fuel cell without a detailed knowledge of 
the underlying physical and electrochemical details. The simplicity and wide acceptance of this developed semi 
empirical model makes it favourable in engineering applications for prediction of V-I characteristics which are 
affected by multiple operational variables such as cell temperature, air pressure and fuel flow rate. However, this 
model is not accurate because it is based on non-mechanistic parameters that are important for optimizing the 
model’s effectiveness4–8. As a result, accurate parameter estimation is critical for the design, simulation, testing, 
and development of fuel cell systems suitable for real time applications.
There are a number of established concepts in the literature that can precisely estimate parameters for Proton 
Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells (PEMFCs). The majority of applied methodologies are optimization based, 
which are simple, consistent and robust9. Many studies have been devoted to the determination of the optimal 
parameters of PEMFCs. For example, a multiverse optimizer has been explored to determine the parameters 
of a PEMFC-equivalent circuit with seven different parameters10. Various optimization parameters which 
ensure effective convergence have been identified by several authors11. These methodologies are categorized as 
evolutionary based, swarm physics, and nature inspired. Various metaheuristics for optimizing microgrids were 
investigated by Hegazy et al.12. Adaptive sparrow search algorithms were used to minimize the sum squared 
error (SSE) to assess the discrepancies between computed and actual voltages13. In14, Yousri et al. concluded 
that the most effective algorithm for mathematically modelling PEMFCs is a fractional order modified Harris 
hawk optimizer. Furthermore, a developed coyote optimization algorithm was used to bridge the gap between 
estimated and empirical results15. Their research was on two types of fuel cells15. Also, the efficacy of an 
enhanced monarch butterfly optimizer was investigated in its application to reduce integral time absolute error 
and identify unknown parameters16. Two types of cells (2 kW Nexa and 6 kW Nedstack PS6) were studied 
under varying conditions with an improved chimp optimizer and validated on three commercial fuel cells with 
a 15-nature algorithm17. An artificial ecosystem based algorithm outperformed the grey wolf optimizer, particle 
swarm optimizer, slime Mold algorithm, and Harris hawk optimizer in terms of outcomes as reported by Tabbi 
et al.18. Additionally, a hybrid method that combines a vortex search algorithm with differential evolution to 
identify optimal PEMFC parameters has been presented19. SSE was used as the ideal fitness function to compare 
experimental voltages with mathematically generated voltages for the stack. A monarch butterfly optimizer 
was also used in experiments on a 250 W PEMFC stack under various conditions20. The optimal parameters 
for PEMFCs were further evaluated by means of metaheuristics21 in order to minimize the SSE between 
experimental and numerical data. Gupta et al. used a slime mold optimizer to find the unknown parameters of 
PEMFCs7, and Qin et al.22 also investigated an enhanced search optimizer for PEMFC parameter evaluation, 
with SSE as the main objective.
Optimal parameters for PEMFCs have been extracted using a Bayesian-regularized neural network23. In 
PEMFCs, Yuan et al.24 used a sunflower optimizer to estimate unknown parameters. In the literature, a converged 
moth search algorithm was highlighted as effective in reducing the SSE between measured and experimental 
voltages, using data from BCS 500 stack and Nedstack PS625. Additionally, a bi-subgroup algorithm has been 
documented for retrieving unknown parameters from PEMFCs26. Syah et al.27applied a balanced strider method 
to minimize the total squared variation between experimental and numerical voltages, with the cost of the stack 
serving as the objective using a modified grass fibrous root algorithm28. For three types of fuel cells (BCS 500/250

two optimizers, the Harris hawk and the atom search algorithm, to estimate unknown values for PEMFCs, 
with SSE as the fitness function30. Rezk et al. used a gradient-based algorithm to determine ideal parameters 
among three types of fuel cells, comparing it against other algorithms31. A chaos owl search optimizer was also 
used to reduce the sum squared deviation for measured and mathematically determined voltages32. A chaotic 
binary shark smell optimizer was implemented for estimating unknown data for a PEMFC33. Furthermore, a 
heterogeneous comprehensive learning Archimedes optimizer was used to find unknown parameters of fuel 
cells34. Artificial neural networks were used in conjunction with a deer hunting algorithm to estimate parameters 
for a PEMFC35. The water cycle algorithm was also used to estimate unknown values for PEMFCs36. It was noted

effective metric to minimize discrepancies between measured and estimated data37. The unknown parameters

been estimated by a satin bowerbird algorithm42. In the literature43, an L-SHADE-EpSin approach was used

The distribution of relaxation times is used by Zuo et al.55 to perform a detailed root cause analysis of proton

Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells (PEMFCs) are modeled using detailed physical and electrochemical 
principles, which results in challenges for mechanistic modeling approaches. However, these models are highly 
dependent on the knowledge of the internal dynamics of the fuel cell, such as reaction kinetics, mass transport 
phenomena, and heat transfer. Although they provide a complete framework for fuel cell behavior, they are 
computationally expensive, very sensitive to parameter changes, and do not easily accommodate changes in 
operational conditions, e.g., fluctuations in temperature, pressure, or humidity. In addition, mechanistic models 
are subject to errors if some parameters are missing or estimated under assumptions. Inadequacies in these 
models can result in deviations from predicted performance, especially under dynamic operating conditions 
where real time adjustments are required. Therefore, such models tend to demonstrate limited scalability and 
generalizability to other types and designs of PEMFC. In contrast, the Two-stage Differential Evolution (TDE) 
algorithm presents an innovative optimization based approach to tackle these deficiencies by performing 
parameter estimation via empirical data fitting. By using observed I/V and P/V characteristics, this method 
reduces computational complexity and improves adaptability. TDE reduces inaccuracies in mechanistic models, 
especially when the system is nonlinear and nonconvex, by optimizing key parameters, such as activation 
voltage drops, concentration losses, and membrane resistance. The empirical foundation of TDE allows it to 
circumvent the need for extensive physical modeling, and provides robust performance over a wide range 
of operational scenarios. However, it is important to note that the success of data driven approaches such as 
TDE relies on having and quality of experimental data. Such methods can be further improved, while both 
theoretically maximally comprehensive and practically applicable, by hybrid models in which mechanistic 
insights and empirical optimization are integrated. The dual approach of this work has the potential to overcome 
existing technology gaps by combining the predictive power of mechanistic models with the adaptability and 
computational efficiency of optimization algorithms to enable real time control and improved system reliability.
In this work, the TDE algorithm is used innovatively to optimize parameters in PEMFC, which is a single 
objective, nonlinear, and non convex optimization problem. The contributions of this study are outlined as 
follows:
•	 Precise identification of PEMFC models based on minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) between actual 
and estimated characteristics, using the TDE along with various DE variants.
•	 An in-depth analysis of the application of DE variants including JADE46, SHADE47, LSHADE48, iLSHADE49, 
CRADE50, jSO51, QUATRE52, LPalmDE53, and HARD-DE54.
•	 Six different commercially available PEMFC stacks were analyzed, including BCS 500 W-PEM58,59, 500W SR-
12PEM60, Nedstak PS6 PEM60, H-12 PEM61, HORIZON 500 W PEM61, and 250 W-stack62.
•	 A full statistical evaluation was conducted to validate the consistency of the methods tested.
•	 The results achieved were benchmarked against findings from existing literature.
In this paper includes the following sections: “Introduction” section introduces Proton Exchange Membrane 
Fuel Cells (PEMFCs) and explains why precise parameter estimation is vital for modeling and optimization 
work. The paper examines traditional optimization difficulties before presenting the Two-Stage Differential 
Evolution (TDE) algorithm as a solution. “Proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) modelling” section 
presents PEMFC mathematical modeling through essential equations which describe reversible voltage together 
with activation voltage drop and ohmic losses and concentration losses. The section introduces the objective

“Differential evolution and two stage differential evolution algorithm” section through an introduction of its 
two-stage mutation strategy and parameter control mechanisms and diversity enhancement techniques. “Result 
analysis” section delivers an extensive results analysis which evaluates TDE performance against state-of-the-
art Differential Evolution (DE) variants through twelve PEMFC case studies. The section presents extensive 
analyses regarding convergence patterns together with error measurement and computational speed. The final 
part of this study concludes with summations and contributions from the TDE algorithm alongside proposed 
research directions for future advancement. The systematic method provides readers with an organized way to 
understand how the TDE algorithm was developed and validated for PEMFC parameter estimation purposes.

Proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) modelling
Basics of the physical operation
Fuel cells are advanced devices designed to convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through an 
electrochemical reaction. Unlike traditional energy systems that rely on combustion and mechanical conversion 
processes, fuel cells provide a clean and efficient alternative. A schematic representation of a conventional Proton 
Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) highlights its key components and operational principles shown in 
Fig. 1. The model comprises two electrodes: the anode, where oxidation occurs, and the cathode, where reduction 
takes place. Positioned between these electrodes are catalyst layers and a proton-conducting membrane.
The system also incorporates two channels dedicated to the delivery of reactants—hydrogen to the anode and 
oxygen (or air) to the cathode. The core functionality of PEMFCs revolves around the electrochemical reactions 
occurring at the electrodes and the transport of ions across the membrane. These processes are fundamental to 
developing mathematical models that accurately represent the physical and chemical behaviors within the cell.
The hydrogen oxidation reaction at the anode, which is a critical step in the PEMFC operation, can be 
represented by the chemical equation63:
	
2H2 + O2 →2H2O 
(1)
Surprisingly, the process yields electrical energy rather than thermal energy, as might be expected from 
conventional combustion.
Anode reaction: At the anode, hydrogen molecules are split into protons (H+) and electrons (e−) through an 
electrochemical process facilitated by a catalyst. This reaction is expressed as:
	
2H2 →4H+ + 4e− 
(2)
The electrons generated in this reaction are directed through an external circuit, producing an electrical current 
that powers external devices.
Cathode reaction: At the cathode, oxygen from the air combines with the incoming electrons from the 
external circuit and protons transported through the membrane. This reaction forms water as the final product, 
represented by the following equation:
	
O2 + 4e−→2H2O 
(3)

PEM fuel cell mathematical model
Mathematical modeling serves as a cornerstone for understanding and optimizing the operation of PEMFCs. 
These models simulate the electrochemical, thermal, and transport phenomena occurring within the fuel cell, 
providing insights into performance and enabling parameter adjustments. A PEMFC stack consists of multiple 
fuel cells connected in series to achieve the desired output. Engineers use these models to evaluate system 
performance and design improvements64.

together with runtime efficiency and statistical indicators that involve SSE minimum and maximum along with 
mean and standard deviation values. The SSE functions as an essential accuracy measurement tool for parameter 
estimation because it measures the difference between experimental and predicted cell voltage readings. The 
model’s fit quality improves as SSE decreases because it demonstrates better experimental data alignment which 
leads to more accurate estimations. Runtime efficiency examines the speed of each algorithm until it reaches 
the optimal solution as measured by computational times. The metric holds special importance in real-time 
applications because it determines both speed and precision of parameter estimation.
Statistical measures give more detailed information about how the algorithms function. The minimum SSE 
shows the most favorable outcome and the maximum SSE demonstrates the least favorable outcome. The mean 
of SSE provides an average performance value over various runs yet standard deviation analysis determines 
algorithm stability where decreased values point to more reliable results. The Friedman ranking72 performs 
non-parametric statistical comparisons between multiple algorithms across various datasets through a results-
ranking method. The ranking system bases its decisions on performance results where the most successful 
algorithm gets the lowest position. The Friedman test serves as an ideal approach to determine overall algorithm 
effectiveness when analyzing multiple case studies.

non-linearity of the PEMFC system, extracting the unknown parameters of its mathematical model presents a 
critical challenge for accurate modeling, design, and control. To address this, voltage–current (V–I) and power-
voltage (P–V) characteristics, influenced by operating temperature and gas pressure, serve as key indicators 
for parameter identification. This work evaluates twelve different PEMFCs based on datasheet specifications, 
applying the recently developed Two-stage Differential Evolution (TDE) algorithm. The performance of TDE is 
compared against several advanced DE variants JADE, SHADE, LSHADE, iLSHADE, CRADE, jSO, QUATRE, 
LPalmDE, and HARD-DE to validate its numerical and statistical robustness. TDE algorithm produced the 
least Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) in all cases where its SSE minimum value reached 0.0255 demonstrating 41% 
better SSE performance than HARD-DE’s value of 0.0432. The TDE algorithm demonstrates robust performance 
through its high accuracy measurements which resulted in a 92% SSE maximum reduction and more than 
99.97% standard deviation decrease. The computational advantages of TDE become evident through its runtime 
efficiency which reaches 0.23 s while HARD-DE requires 11.95 s. The proposed model together with its tuning 
methodology achieves validation through successful experimental data alignment with all twelve case studies for 
both I/V and P/V characteristics. The TDE algorithm demonstrates reliable PEMFC prediction capability across 
different operating conditions that involve stack temperature as well as oxygen and hydrogen partial pressure 
modifications. Use of TDE yielded optimized parameters which accurately performed on the nonlinear structure 
of PEMFC systems.
The model prediction capability across diverse operating conditions will be improved through this 
approach as it allows identical parameter utilization for a wide range of PEMFC scenarios thus boosting real-
time applications. The TDE algorithm demonstrates its effectiveness through successful minimization of SSE, 
Absolute Error (AE), Relative Error (RE) and Mean Bias Error (MBE) in all cases. The algorithm demonstrates 
valuable characteristics of precision along with stability and computational efficiency which make it suitable for 
research and industrial applications. Electronic component simulators can benefit from TDE implementation 
to enable PEMFC device analysis for enhancing fuel cell system efficiency and reliability. The TDE algorithm 
delivers a major progress in PEMFC parameter estimation technology by bringing forth a dependable and 
efficient computational method for precise modeling and control purposes.
Future work will integrate multiple fuel cell cases with different operating conditions into a unified 
optimization process to validate the model. The optimization process will unite model parameters for cases 6, 
8, 9, and 10 because these cases use the same fuel cell type under different operating conditions. The analysis 
will treat cases 4, 11 and 12 as one group. The researchers will pursue two main objectives in future studies 
regarding TDE algorithms by investigating broader applicability to different fuel cells while developing real-time 
data analysis along with hybrid machine learning methods. The efforts will enhance the wider adoption of clean 
energy technologies and optimize fuel cell system performance.
